title: SQL Fundamentals
tagline: query plans, indexes, dialect nuances — optimization begins

placementQuiz.q: An Index Scan is generally faster than Seq Scan because:
options: It reads fewer pages by jumping via B-tree
It uses more CPU but less I/O
It only works on primary keys
placementQuiz.explain: B-tree index lets the database jump directly to matching rows instead of scanning all pages.

options: Cost is 0.29 for index, 42.15 for table
placementQuiz.explain: Cost is planner's estimate in arbitrary units. First = startup, second = total.

placementQuiz.q: Which index type supports range queries (>, <, BETWEEN) efficiently?
placementQuiz.explain: B-tree maintains sorted order, enabling range scans. Hash only supports equality.

placementQuiz.q: Partial index (WHERE clause on index) is useful when:
options: You always query the same subset (e.g., status='active')
placementQuiz.explain: Partial index only indexes rows matching condition — smaller, faster for that subset.
INCLUDE columns stored in index leaf — query satisfied from index alone, no heap fetch.

sections.title: Query Plans Deep Dive — EXPLAIN ANALYZE

blocks.md: **EXPLAIN shows the plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and shows actuals. Compare estimated vs actual rows — divergence = stale stats or bad assumptions.**

blocks.label: explain variants
blocks.pg:
-- PostgreSQL specific options
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON) SELECT ...;

blocks.title: Seq Scan with Filter (Actual vs Estimated)

blocks.md: **Estimated rows: 8500 → Actual: 3200.** Statistics may be stale (run ANALYZE) or filter selectivity misestimated. At L4 you'll learn to fix this with extended statistics.

items.explain: Planner relies on pg_stats. Stale stats = wrong row estimates = bad plan choices.
Shared hit = pages already in RAM. Shared read = disk I/O. Dirtied = modified.

blocks.label: btree usage
blocks.code:
-- Created automatically for PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE
-- Manual creation
CREATE INDEX idx_employees_salary ON employees (salary);

-- Composite (order matters!)
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_dept_salary ON employees (dept_id, salary);

-- Supports: =, <, >, <=, >=, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE 'prefix%'
-- Does NOT support: LIKE '%suffix', functions on column

blocks.md: Hash indexes only support `=` comparisons. Faster for point lookups but no range scans. PostgreSQL: `CREATE INDEX ... USING HASH`. MySQL MEMORY engine uses hash by default.

items: **GIN** — Generalized Inverted Index: arrays, JSONB, full-text search, `col @> '{"key": "val"}'`
**GiST** — Generalized Search Tree: geometric data, `tsvector`, range types
**BRIN** — Block Range Index: huge tables with natural correlation (timestamps, auto-increment IDs). Tiny size, coarse granularity.
**SP-GiST** — Space-Partitioned GiST: non-balanced structures (quadtrees, prefix trees)

items.explain: GIN is designed for composite values with containment/overlap operators.

options: Huge tables with correlated columns (time, ID)
items.explain: BRIN stores min/max per block range. Tiny (KB vs GB) but only works when physical order matches logical.

sections.title: Index Pitfalls — When Indexes Don't Help

blocks.label: functions on columns kill indexes
blocks.pg:
-- Functional index (PostgreSQL)
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_upper_name ON employees (UPPER(name));
blocks.mysql:
-- Functional index (MySQL 8.0+)
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_upper_name ON employees ((UPPER(name)));

blocks.label: leading wildcard kills index

blocks.md: **Low selectivity = planner ignores index.** If query returns >5-10% of table, Seq Scan is often faster (sequential I/O vs random). Check `reltuples` vs `rows` in EXPLAIN.

items.q: WHERE UPPER(name) = 'ALICE' ignores index on name because:
options: Function on column prevents B-tree usage
items.explain: B-tree stores raw column values. Function transforms value → can't traverse tree. Fix: functional index.

items.q: Planner chooses Seq Scan over Index Scan when:
options: Query returns large fraction of table (>5-10%)
items.explain: Random I/O (index) vs sequential I/O (scan). Threshold depends on settings (random_page_cost).

items.title: Create Index for Salary Range Queries
items.statement: Create a B-tree index on employees.salary to speed up range queries.

items.title: Composite Index for Dept + Salary
items.statement: Create composite index for queries filtering by dept_id then ordering by salary.
hints: Column order matters: equality first (dept_id), then range (salary)

items.title: Partial Index for Active Employees
items.statement: 90% of queries filter status='active'. Create partial index on salary for active employees only.

items.title: Covering Index to Avoid Heap Fetch
items.statement: Query: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000. Create covering index.
hints: INCLUDE (name) in PostgreSQL; (salary, name) in MySQL

items.title: Analyze Query Plan
items.statement: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE dept_id = 3 AND salary > 60000. Note: Seq Scan vs Index Scan, actual rows.

items.statement: Query: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE LOWER(email) = 'alice@company.com'. Create index to support this.

revisionCard: EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE — estimated vs actual rows reveals stats issues
B-tree = default, supports ranges; Hash = equality only; GIN = JSONB/arrays; BRIN = huge correlated tables
Partial index (WHERE on index) for skewed query patterns
Functions on columns kill indexes — use functional indexes
Leading wildcard (%text) kills B-tree — pg_trgm or fulltext for that

glossary.def: Index that includes all columns needed by query (INCLUDE), avoiding table lookup.
Index with WHERE clause — only indexes subset of rows.
Index on expression (e.g., UPPER(col)) — supports queries with functions.
Fraction of rows matching condition. Low selectivity = few rows = index friendly.
Table lookup after index finds row pointer. Covering index eliminates this.
Planner parameter: cost of random I/O vs sequential. Higher = prefer Seq Scan.
